data.name: Ishin no Arashi
data.detailed_description:
To commemorate Kou Shibusawa's 35th anniversary, the "Kou Shibusawa Archives" will be opened in the Steam Store. Here we will revive popular previously released titles.

In this fourth round of releases, we offer "Ishin no Arashi," released in 1988. Its story takes place at the end of the Tokugawa Shogunate. Players become one of the 12 key figures of the time, like Ryoma Sakamoto, Kaishu Katsu, and Takamori Saigo. They guide Japan to freedom by using persuasion and force to unify the 13 domains under one ideal, whether that is loyalty to the shogunate or the emperor, or even to the public opinion.

reviews.review:
*Ishin no Arashi*, developed and published by KOEI TECMO GAMES CO., LTD., is a deeply rooted historical simulation that reflects the early ambitions of Koei’s strategy design long before the genre became more streamlined and accessible. Set during the volatile Bakumatsu era of Japan, the game places players in the midst of a nation on the brink of transformation, where political ideology, personal ambition, and shifting alliances all collide. Rather than focusing purely on warfare or territorial expansion, it attempts to simulate the broader social and ideological upheaval of the time, giving it a distinctly intellectual and methodical tone.

What makes the game particularly notable is its character-driven approach. Players assume the role of one of several historical figures, each with their own abilities, affiliations, and ideological leanings. Instead of commanding faceless armies, you are navigating a network of individuals whose loyalty and beliefs matter just as much as their strength. This creates a more personal form of strategy, where building relationships, persuading others, and aligning yourself with the right factions can be just as impactful as engaging in conflict. The game places a strong emphasis on influence—how it is gained, how it is used, and how it shapes the direction of events.

The gameplay itself blends elements of role-playing with grand strategy, resulting in a system that can feel both expansive and demanding. Players manage their character’s development, travel between locations, engage in discussions, and participate in political maneuvering, all while keeping an eye on the broader state of the nation. Decisions are rarely straightforward, as they often involve balancing immediate benefits against long-term consequences. The ideological divide between maintaining the shogunate, restoring imperial authority, or embracing foreign influence adds another layer of complexity, turning the game into a kind of interactive historical thought experiment. It’s less about winning in a conventional sense and more about shaping outcomes in a way that aligns with your chosen path.

One of the defining features of *Ishin no Arashi* is its open-ended structure. The game does not strictly follow historical events; instead, it allows them to unfold dynamically based on player actions. This means that familiar historical milestones can occur differently—or not at all—depending on how the player influences the world. While this freedom is one of the game’s greatest strengths, it also contributes to a sense of ambiguity. There is little in the way of direct guidance, and players are often left to interpret systems and objectives on their own. This can be rewarding for those who enjoy experimentation, but it may feel overwhelming for newcomers.

The presentation reflects its origins as a much older title. Visually, it is functional rather than engaging, with a heavy reliance on menus and text to convey information. The interface can be difficult to navigate at first, lacking the clarity and convenience that modern strategy games typically provide. Learning how to effectively interact with the game’s systems requires patience, as many mechanics are not immediately intuitive. The pacing is similarly deliberate, emphasizing gradual progress and long-term planning rather than quick results. This slower tempo reinforces the game’s simulation focus but can also make it feel dense and inaccessible to those expecting a more dynamic experience.

Despite these challenges, there is a remarkable depth to the systems at play. The way personal attributes, relationships, and political dynamics intertwine creates a simulation that feels surprisingly nuanced, even by modern standards. Every decision carries weight, and the consequences of your actions can ripple outward in unexpected ways. This level of complexity is not always easy to appreciate, especially given the dated presentation, but it rewards players who are willing to invest the time to understand it.

Ultimately, *Ishin no Arashi* is less about immediate enjoyment and more about immersion in a historical and strategic framework. It stands as a precursor to many of Koei’s later successes, showcasing ideas that would eventually be refined into more accessible forms. For modern players, it can feel archaic and demanding, but for those with an interest in historical simulations or the evolution of strategy games, it offers a uniquely thoughtful and challenging experience.

Rating: 6/10
